Sam chats with Stacey Vanek Smith, host of NPR's The Indicator , and Cardiff Garcia, former co-host of The Indicator , about the American job market and why businesses are having such a hard time hiring. Then, as vaccines have become more widely available and pandemic restrictions lift across the country, people are wandering back out into the world, having experiences they haven't had in over a year. We drop in on a few of these: a dance party, a first date, a game with friends — the small pleasures folks have missed that now feel monumental.

title: Housing Boom For Whom? Plus, 'Ziwe' Premieres
standfirst: The housing market is booming— but who actually benefits? Sam talks to Jerusalem Demsas, politics and policy fellow for Vox, about what so many are getting wrong about housing. Plus, Sam revisits his 2020 conversation with Ziwe Fumudoh, whose comedy variety show Ziwe premieres on Showtime on May 9. Then, in honor of NPR's 50th anniversary, Sam plays "Who Said That?" with All Things Considered hosts Audie Cornish and Ari Shapiro.

title: Jobs Friday And The Labor Market Mystery
standfirst: Unemployment is still above 6%, but companies across the US are saying they can't find people to fill their jobs. What's going on?

title: Good jobs Friday
standfirst: The US economy added more than 200,000 jobs in June. But are these good jobs? Today, we look at some ways to answer this question, and what it takes to transform a job from bad to good.

title: An economic argument for heat safety regulation (Encore)
standfirst: It's been a summer of record breaking heat. And for both outdoor and indoor workers, that heat poses a growing health risk. Around the country, worker advocates and industry groups are in an ongoing fight over how to address extreme heat and workplace safety. And that got The Indicator team thinking about an episode we did last year.

title: What to know about the drug price fight in those TV ads
standfirst: At least nine bills introduced in Congress take aim at pharmacy benefit managers, the powerful middlemen that channel prescription drugs to patients. Here's what the fuss is all about.

title: Inflation may be cooling, but the housing market is still too hot for many buyers
standfirst: The median home price has risen to $413,800 – the second-highest price ever — thanks to a shortage of homes on the market and high mortgage rates. Experts say renting may be a better option.

title: Biden frames his clean energy plan as a jobs plan, obscuring his record on climate
standfirst: President Biden's Inflation Reduction Act invests $369 billion to address the climate crisis. But as the president focuses on the law's economic benefits, is his climate win getting lost?

title: Biden administration proposes new fuel economy standards, with higher bar for trucks
standfirst: The proposal would increase fuel economy for cars by 2% annually — and twice as fast for trucks and SUVs. The rule would pair with the EPA's ambitious plan to promote electric vehicles.

title: The job market is cooling but still surprisingly strong. Is that a good thing?
standfirst: U.S. employers added 209,000 jobs in June. That's a solid number, but fewer than the month before. Here are the 5 things we took away from the report.

title: AMC Theaters reverses its decision to price tickets based on where customers sit
standfirst: The company said the new pricing structure made the cost of their tickets less competitive in the market.

title: Inflation eases to its lowest in over two years, but it's still running a bit high
standfirst: Consumer inflation hit 3% in June, the lowest since March 2021. Though easing prices will be comforting to the Federal Reserve, inflation is still running higher than the central bank would like.

title: Why inflation is losing its punch — and why things could get even better
standfirst: Annual inflation fell to 3% in June, the lowest since March 2021. That probably won't stop the Federal Reserve from raising rates again, but this month's expected hike could be the last.

title: IRS, Ivies and GDP
standfirst: In this edition of Indicators of the Week, we talk about the end of surprise IRS visits, new research on elite college admissions, and why a soft landing is in sight.

title: What recession? It's a summer of splurging, profits and girl power
standfirst: Economic data show higher prices and constant warnings of a downturn haven't slowed down American shoppers. The Fed is anxious. Companies are thrilled.

title: The U.S. added 209,000 jobs in June, showing that hiring is slowing but still solid
standfirst: U.S. employers added 209,000 jobs in June, marking another respectable month of job growth, though it was slower than in previous months.

title: The case for a soft landing in the economy just got another boost
standfirst: U.S. employers added 187,000 jobs in July, a slower but still solid pace of growth, suggesting the Federal Reserve may be able to curb inflation without triggering a recession.

title: When mortgage rates are too low to give up
standfirst: The average mortgage rate in the U.S. just hit 7.09%—its highest level in more than two decades. And that's having ripple effects in the wider economy. Some homeowners feel locked in, tethered to their super low interest rates and unable to find something better. Today on the show, what happens when homeowners are locked in by low rates?

title: Farm Jobs Friday
standfirst: Farm employment numbers are historically very hard to track. Partly because they fluctuate a lot from season to season, partly because a large portion of farm workers are undocumented. They're also not included in the monthly job numbers, which means we hardly ever talk about them on Jobs Friday. But today we're bringing you "Farm Jobs Friday" as we zoom in on three big trends in farm employment.

title: Being in between jobs is normal. Here's how to talk about it
standfirst: I recently went on medical leave from my job. I'm looking for a new career start and working through options. How can I talk about my in-between career state with friends and family?

title: A tarot card reading for the U.S. economy
standfirst: Predicting the future of the economy is always a dicey proposition. That is especially true after more than three years of pandemic-related economic weirdness. No one quite knows what will happen next.

title: The U.S. added jobs at a solid pace in July, reinforcing hopes about the economy
standfirst: U.S. employers added 187,000 jobs in July, still marking a steady pace of growth. The unemployment rate edged down to 3.5%.

title: Janet Yellen says a government shutdown would add to risks of a recession
standfirst: Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen is sounding the alarm about the damage a government shutdown could do to the U.S. economy. "It's really reckless and will impose immediate harm," Yellen told NPR.

title: The Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady but hints at more action this year
standfirst: The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged Wednesday, despite stubborn inflation, although it left the door open to an additional rate hike in November or December.

title: What a crop of upcoming IPOs from Birkenstock to Instacart tells us about the economy
standfirst: A crop of IPOs are coming, starting with chip designer Arm, which is making its debut on Thursday. It's another sign of confidence in markets — and the U.S. economy.

title: Sky-high CEO pay is in focus as workers everywhere are demanding higher wages
standfirst: As autoworkers' real wages fall, top executives at the Big Three carmakers continue to earn tens of millions of dollars each year — hundreds of times more than the median employee.

title: How to make sense of the country's stunningly strong job market
standfirst: U.S. employers added about twice as many jobs in September as forecasters expected. That's good for people looking for work, but the strong report could complicate the Fed's effort to curb inflation.

title: Junk fees, unfilled jobs, jackpot
standfirst: On this edition of Indicators of the Week: the FTC wants to ban hidden fees on what feels like every transaction. Down with junk fees! Germany has a possible fix for its struggling economy and unfilled jobs: immigrants. And we explore why the Powerball jackpots keep getting so big.

title: The job market was stunningly strong in September
standfirst: Employers added 336,000 jobs in September, far more than expected. It's good news for people looking for work, but the strong labor market could complicate the Fed's fight against inflation.

title: Inflation has a new victim: Girl Scout cookies
standfirst: Many Girl Scout councils are raising the price of their popular cookies from $5 to $6 a box. The increase offers Girl Scouts and their customers a bittersweet lesson in inflation.

title: Indicator exploder: jobs and inflation
standfirst: When someone says "the economy is doing well"—what does that even mean? Like, for workers, for employers, for the country as a whole? According to what calculation? How do you put a number on it?

title: 5 things to know about a stunning week for the economy
standfirst: The U.S. economy continues to defy gravity, growing rapidly despite high interest rates. Consumer spending is powering the expansion, but it's not clear how long that can last.

title: Social Security recipients will get a smaller increase in benefits as inflation cools
standfirst: Social Security beneficiaries will receive a 3.2% cost of living adjustment next year. Inflation has been moderating recently, with consumer prices in September up 3.7% from a year ago.

title: Netflix raises prices for its premium plan
standfirst: Netflix said it's raising the price for its most expensive streaming service by $2 to $23 per month in the U.S., and its lowest-priced, ad-free streaming plan to $12 — another $2 bump.

title: Body Electric: What digital jobs are doing to our bodies
standfirst: TED Radio Hour's Manoush Zamorodi joins us today to talk about her new series Body Electric. It's looking at how the information age is affecting our bodies in negative ways.

title: A bad economy can be good for your health
standfirst: When economist Chris Ruhm first got the results from his study on the possible connection between recession and health, he thought he had made a mistake. But time and time again, he got the same results, overturning a decade of previous economic findings. Today, how a nation's health relates to your own.

title: Economic fact in literary fiction
standfirst: Some of the most influential and beloved novels of the last few years have been about money, finance, and the global economy. Some overtly so, others more subtly. It got to the point where we just had to call up the authors to find out more: What brought them into this world? What did they learn? How were they thinking about economics when they wrote these beautiful books?

title: As gasoline prices fall, U.S. inflation cools to 3.2%
standfirst: Consumer prices last month were 3.2% higher than the month before — a smaller annual increase than the previous month. A sharp drop in gas prices in October helped to offset rising rents.

title: Prices fall, unemployment rises and Boomers have all the houses
standfirst: We've been on a wild economic ride lately so let's find the key trends to make sense of where the economy's headed. On this edition of Indicators of the Week, the numbers you need to know about falling producer prices, rising unemployment claims and generational home-buying trends.

title: Starbucks increases U.S. hourly wages and adds other benefits for non-union workers
standfirst: The company said Monday unionized workers won't be eligible for some of those perks, a sign of the continuing tension between the Seattle coffee giant and the union trying to organize its U.S. stores.

title: Why everyone in the labor market is being picky
standfirst: The American economy is still running hot and the labor market is showing astounding resilience despite elevated interest rates. Things are so good that there's some pickiness being displayed by both employers and employees. Today, we look at what's turning out to be an unusual labor market and what that means for the wider economy.

title: The 'R' word: Why this time might be an exception to a key recession rule
standfirst: The author of the 'Sahm Rule' is less worried about rising unemployment this time, even though October's rate was up 0.5% from a recent low...a jump typically associated with the onset of recession.

title: Tough housing market is luring buyers without kids and higher incomes
standfirst: A report from the National Association of Realtors shows the average home buyer this past year had a six-figure income. Others face challenges in a period of high prices and costly home loans.

title: Americans don't like higher prices but they LOVE buying new things
standfirst: Eight times a year, regional Federal Reserve Banks release a collection of anecdotes that reveal stories about the economy. These stories come together in what's known as the "Beige Book," and we award the regional bank with the best entry with our coveted Beigie Award. Today, we're highlighting an entry that gets to the heart of the contradictions we're seeing when it comes to consumer preferences and sentiment.

title: How rock-bottom prices drive shortages of generic drugs used in hospitals
standfirst: Hospitals rely on scores of generic drugs given by injection. But these workhorses are often in short supply. Cheap prices have led to factory closures that leave the supply chain vulnerable.

title: Why corporate bankruptcies were up in 2023 despite the improving economy
standfirst: Hundreds of debt-saddled companies filed for bankruptcy this year, as the era of easy money caught up to corporations. High interest rates mean banks aren't extending lifelines.

title: The Fed is probably done raising interest rates and could cut them next year
standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, amid signs of easing inflation. The central bank signaled that its benchmark borrowing rate may start to fall next year.

title: The 'physics' behind potential interest rate cuts
standfirst: In the world of science there are laws—rules that describe how the universe works. The Federal Reserve has its own set of rules, except its rules are more like guidelines to help the Fed decide where interest rates should be. Today on the show, we explain inertial and non-inertial rules in the world of monetary policy, and what they tell us about potential rate cuts in the year ahead.

title: Where the Republican presidential candidates stand on the economy
standfirst: GOP presidential hopefuls know that the economy is an important issue — if not the top issue — for voters. That means it's a big talker on the campaign trail and a focus area for winning votes.

title: UPS is cutting 12,000 jobs just months after reaching union deal
standfirst: UPS will cut 12,000 jobs and released a revenue outlook for this year that sent its shares down sharply. CEO Carol Tome said that the job cuts will produce $1 billion in cost savings.

title: How to transform a war economy for peacetime
standfirst: In the 1980s, California was the heart of the aerospace industry. But when the Cold War ended, military spending cuts put those defense jobs in jeopardy.

title: The Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady but signals rate cuts may be coming
standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, but indicated that rates could fall in the coming months if inflation continues to cool.

title: Higher wages, fewer temp workers and indicators of the year results
standfirst: The U.S. economy added a solid number of jobs, the unemployment rate held steady, and a lot of people got raises. But, today we ask whether fewer temporary workers could mean recession, and whether higher wages might cause interest rates to stay high.

title: U.S. unemployment has been under 4% for the longest streak since the Vietnam War
standfirst: U.S. employers added 216,000 jobs in December, as the unemployment rate held steady at 3.7%. The labor market proved resilient in 2023, despite rising interest rates.

title: Sushi restaurants are thriving in Ukraine, bringing jobs and a 'slice of normal life'
standfirst: Ukraine's economy is battered by Russia's full-scale invasion, but its consumer economy is still running — especially the country's popular sushi restaurants, where cream cheese is a key ingredient.

title: The S&P 500 surges to a record high as hopes about the economy — and Big Tech — grow
standfirst: The index surged over 1% to hit a record high, surpassing the previous peak hit around two years ago, driven by big gains in large tech companies and by hopes about the economy.

title: As car insurance continues to rise, U.S. inflation ticks up in December
standfirst: Overall CPI in December was up 3.4% from a year ago. The cost of motor vehicle insurance rose 1.5% in December from November, marking a 20.3% increase compared to the previous year.

title: Cocoa prices spiked to an all-time high right before Valentine's Day
standfirst: Chocolate lovers won't see a sudden price spike for Valentine's Day — because the cost already has been rising for months. Extreme weather is largely to blame.

title: Here's a big reason why people may be gloomy about the economy: the cost of money
standfirst: Former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers argues that high interest rates are contributing to people's gloomy economic mood. Sentiment may improve, though, if the Federal Reserve begins to cut rates.

title: How local government is propping up the U.S. labor market
standfirst: The most recent jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows the United States economy exceeded expectations by adding 353,000 jobs in January. This continues the labor market's years-long trend of resilience in the face of the Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes. However, digging deeper into the numbers reveals figures that economists are keeping a close eye on.

title: How Egypt's military is dragging down its economy
standfirst: Egypt's economy is facing its worst crisis in decades. The situation could further destabilize the Middle East if it goes unresolved. Now, the International Monetary Fund is working with Egyptian leadership to figure out another deal for a multi-billion dollar loan ... but will it be enough? Today, we look at how Egypt has fallen into economic crisis and whether its economy is too big to fail.

title: Donor gives $40 million for Yellowstone National Park employee housing
standfirst: Yellowstone employs more than 3,000 people at peak season, finding enough affordable housing for them has long been a problem.

title: How are moving companies faring with high mortgage rates?
standfirst: HOOAH! It's our first Beigie Award for 2024! The Beigie Award is back to recognize the regional Federal Reserve Bank with the best Beige Book entry. This edition's winner took us to the City of Brotherly Love, detailing how high home interest rates and low existing home sales in the area are financially affecting our buff brethren in arms: movers.

title: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady, projects three rate cuts later this year
standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday, but policymakers signaled they still expect to start cutting rates later this year. The stock market jumped in response.

title: California fast-food workers will get $20 minimum wage, starting Monday
standfirst: Debate is hot about the impact of a higher minimum wage. Half a million Californians work in fast-food, where wages had stagnated for decades. Restaurant owners warn of higher prices and fewer hours.

title: When does youth employment become child labor?
standfirst: The number of teenagers in the workforce today is at its highest level in about 20 years. At the same time, child labor violations are up and states are relaxing some protections for their youngest workers. On today's show, we examine the state of the Gen Z labor force, and the distinction between youth employment and child labor.

title: Reddit stock starts trading 38% above initial public offering price
standfirst: Reddit, the San Francisco social media site that describes itself as "the front page of the internet," is debuting as a public stock on Thursday.

title: Wages, employment, inflation are up, causing headaches for the Fed
standfirst: The Federal Reserve is expected to hold interest rates steady this week — and possibly for months to come — as policymakers try to sort through mixed signals about the U.S. economy.

title: Housing costs keep inflation stubborn; New report on Maui wildfires released
standfirst: Inflation is proving stubborn this year, and the cost of rent may be to blame. Hawaii's attorney general has released the first report into last year's Maui fires.

title: Taiwan earthquake briefly halts chip factories that power the global economy
standfirst: The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., which makes more than 90% of world's most advanced chips, also halted production, but it plans to resume chipmaking overnight.

title: What Subway's foot-long cookie says about inflation
standfirst: In this edition of Indicators of the Week: the new incentive for speed in cash prizes for Olympic track and field, growing iPhone assembly in India and the curious inflation puzzle of the foot-long cookies at Subway.

title: No more 'just walk out' at Amazon grocery stores. The new bet is smart shopping carts
standfirst: The retailer banked big on the cashier-less tech. It's now out at Amazon Fresh stores in the U.S. But Amazon's grocery ambitions are only shapeshifting.

title: 6 months into war, Palestinians face high unemployment and a 'disastrous' economy
standfirst: A Palestinian Authority official says there are around 700,000 Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza who have gone six months without work since the war between Israel and Hamas began on Oct. 7.

title: The Forever Stamp just went up in price. How does the U.S. cost compare globally?
standfirst: U.S. stamps just had their sixth price hike since 2021. In raw numbers, only four countries in a recent study of 31 developed nations had cheaper stamps than the U.S.

title: Tesla cuts its car prices around the world after week of turmoil for the company
standfirst: The company dropped its starting prices of its Model X, Model Y and Model S by $2,000 in the U.S.

title: Amazon is cutting hundreds of jobs in its cloud computing unit AWS
standfirst: The AWS layoffs follow other layoffs that happened at Amazon and its subsidiaries this year, including at Prime Video, the MGM Studios unit and Twitch, the social media platform owned by Amazon.

title: White-sounding names get called back for jobs more than Black ones, a new study finds
standfirst: Economists sent 83,000 fake job applications to a slew of major U.S. companies, and found that the typical firm favored white applicants over Black ones by around 9%.

title: 'Wall Street Journal' layoffs continue, despite lucrative AI deal and record profits
standfirst: The Wall Street Journal conducted another round of layoffs, explaining that it was pulling back from regional and local general news. It already has cut staff in Washington and abroad.

title: How the Dominican Republic became Latin America's economic superstar
standfirst: For decades, the Dominican Republic's economy has been growing at a remarkably steady pace. The Caribbean nation of 11 million people is today considered a middle-income nation, but the International Monetary Fund projects it could become an advanced economy within the next 40 years.

title: The highs and lows of US rents
standfirst: The latest inflation numbers are in. This month's Consumer Price Index, or the CPI, is ... well, good and bad news for renters. Shelter prices went up over the last year, but at a slower pace. Shelter makes up nearly a third of the CPI. Today's episode: Rent. Where is it high? Where is it low? What exactly is "coffee milk"? The Indicator tours the U.S. to bring you the answers.

title: Biden will keep Trump's China tariffs, and add new ones on electric vehicles
standfirst: The Biden administration is finally wrapping up its review of President Donald Trump's tariffs on Chinese imports. It will keep those tariffs, and add more on things like electric vehicles.

title: Target is cutting prices on 5,000 items including milk, butter and pet food
standfirst: Target joins other retailers trying to draw inflation-weary shoppers to stores. The chain says reductions have already been reflected in about 1,500 products.

title: Not too hot, not too cold: a 'Goldilocks' jobs report
standfirst: It's Jobs Friday and the jobs report is in! There's more jobs! ... but not as many as expected. And there's a teensy bit more unemployment and slower wage growth. But there's an upside ... Plus, healthcare is growing like gangbusters and how immigrants affect American-born workers.

title: Biden announces new tariffs on imports of Chinese goods, including electric vehicles
standfirst: President Biden is keeping the tariffs on Chinese imports put in place by his predecessor and 2024 opponent, former President Donald Trump. And he's adding new ones for things like electric vehicles.

title: Possible TikTok ban could be 'an extinction-level event' for the creator economy
standfirst: Tens of thousands of people earn a living on TikTok. But as creators face down the real possibility of TikTok going away, many are trying to switch to new platforms to save their livlihoods.

title: 5 takeaways from Biden's tariff hikes on Chinese electric vehicles
standfirst: The Biden administration is quadrupling tariffs on China-made EVs. The tariffs are part of a broad swath of protectionist policies first imposed by former President Trump.

title: The Fed holds rates steady, sees only one rate cut in 2024 as inflation cools slowly
standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady while signaling it can cut rates only once this year. The decision came after data earlier showed inflation cooling slightly.

title: A captive market: The high price of prison phone calls
standfirst: When Diane Lewis' son, Jovaan, was sentenced to prison, she told him to call her every day. What he didn't know at the time is that those collect calls often meant Diane was unable to pay her other bills. Today on the show, how prison phone calls got so expensive, and the movement to make them free.

title: Hiring jumps in May but so does unemployment
standfirst: U.S. employers added 272,000 jobs in May -- more than forecasters had expected. The unemployment rate inched up to 4% from 3.9% in April.

title: U.S. home prices have far outpaced paychecks. See what it looks like where you live
standfirst: In nearly half of metro areas, buyers must make more than $100,000 to afford a median-priced home, a Harvard University report finds. And home prices this year reached a new all-time high.

title: Bringing a tariff to a graphite fight
standfirst: Graphite is sort of the one-hit wonder of minerals. And that hit? Pencils. Everyone loves to talk about pencils when it comes to graphite. If graphite were to perform a concert, they'd close out the show with "pencils," and everyone would clap and cheer. But true fans of graphite would be shouting out "batteries!" Because graphite is a key ingredient in another important thing that we all use in our everyday lives: lithium ion batteries.

title: Do immigrants really take jobs and lower wages?
standfirst: We wade into the heated debate over immigrants' impact on the labor market. When the number of workers in a city increases, does that take away jobs from the people who already live and work there? Does a surge of immigration hurt their wages?

title: Ghost jobs
standfirst: Today's jobs report shows a slight rise in unemployment to 4%. And some frustrated job seekers are growing tired of applying for job after job with no replies, sometimes asking whether the listings are even real. And this isn't just vexing for applicants. It's also haunting economists when trying to figure out how much slack there is in the labor market, and whether interest rates should be raised or lowered. Today on the show: the rise of ghost jobs. Where they're happening and why.

title: To help the economy, an Alabama county is betting on home-based child care
standfirst: A project in Alabama seeks to drastically grow the number of home-based child care options. It could help the state's workforce, especially during nontraditional hours.

title: If AI is so good, why are there still so many jobs for translators?
standfirst: Machine translation of foreign languages has been good for a while. And yet human translators are still in demand. Why isn’t AI killing these jobs? And even if it isn’t, how is it reshaping them?

title: Common economic myths, debunked
standfirst: Maybe you've heard these things on social media, in the news, and take them as fact: More than half of the adults in the US live paycheck to paycheck, the trade deficit is always bad, and making the super wealthy pay their fair share will fix everything .

title: What's with all the tiny soda cans? And other grocery store mysteries, solved.
standfirst: There's a behind the scenes industry that helps big brands decide questions like: How big should a bag of chips be? What's the right size for a bottle of shampoo? And yes, also: When should a company do a little shrinkflation?

title: Food prices are no longer rising as much — but here's why it might not feel that way
standfirst: Food prices have largely leveled off, but many people are still frustrated when they go to their local grocery store.

title: Do you rent? You may be more vulnerable to climate-driven disasters
standfirst: The financial cards are stacked against many renters who survive hurricanes, floods, wildfires and other major weather disasters. The long-term effects can be devastating.

title: The Federal Reserve is getting closer to cutting interest rates
standfirst: The Fed kept interest rates unchanged at the highest in more than two decades. Investors are betting it will start to lower rates at its next meeting in September.

title: America's startup boom is still going strong. Here's what it means for the economy
standfirst: Four years ago, Americans began creating new businesses at a record rate. The boom is still here, and it could be a great sign for the U.S. economy.

title: The two companies driving the modern economy
standfirst: At the core of most of the electronics we use today are some very tiny, very powerful chips. Semiconductor chips. And they are mighty: they help power our phones, laptops, and cars. They enable advances in healthcare, military systems, transportation, and clean energy. And they're also critical for artificial intelligence, providing the hardware needed to train complex machine learning.

title: Are both rents AND interest rates too dang high?
standfirst: The Federal Reserve has once again opted to leave interest rates unchanged. That appears to be creating a big challenge to one part of the economy: housing prices. Today, we look at how elevated interest rates may actually be keeping home prices and rent high. Plus, we see how one community is taking the issue of housing affordability into its own hands.

title: One of the hottest jobs in AI right now: 'types-question guy'
standfirst: U.S. job growth cooled this month. But one job is hot to the touch: AI prompt engineer. The role can command a six figure salary, but ... what is it? Today, we speak to an AI prompt engineer to figure out what they actually do and how long the job could remain hot.

title: How much do presidents ACTUALLY influence the economy?
standfirst: Voters have a bleak outlook on the economy right now, and many are pointing the finger at President Biden. At the same time, many voters have a rosy view of the economy when Donald Trump was president. But how much credit or blame should a president get for the economy? And how do partisan politics play into our perception of the economy's performance?

title: What has helped you afford housing in this market? We want to hear from you
standfirst: Record numbers of Americans face unaffordable rent and home prices. If you’re among them, please tell us about the sacrifices or creative solutions this has meant for you.

title: How to fix a housing shortage
standfirst: When Cody Fischer decided to get into real estate development, he had a vision. He wanted to build affordable, energy efficient apartments in Minneapolis, not far from where he grew up.

title: How mortgage interest rates work (and why they're currently out of whack)
standfirst: Even with falling interest rates in recent weeks, mortgage rates are still higher than you'd expect.

title: Quiz: Do you know your economic history?
standfirst: Time to show your economic history skills based on what we’ve covered in Planet Money Summer School 2024: An Incomplete Economic History of the World. Make it through the quiz, and receive a — and we cannot stress this enough — totally fake (yet well-earned) diploma.

title: Summer School 7: The Great Depression, the New Deal and how it changed our economy
standfirst: Find all the episodes from this season here. And past seasons here. And follow along on TikTok here for video Summer School.

title: U.S. added fewer jobs in the past year than initially reported
standfirst: A preliminary report from the Labor Department shows U.S. employers added 818,000 fewer jobs in the year ending in March than initially reported. The news comes during an election season in which the economy is a key issue.

title: The Economic Mind of Tim Walz
standfirst: A rundown on some of the Democratic VP candidate’s important economic policy decisions.

title: Best of Life Kit: Tips on how to deal with cheaters, cut food costs and split baby care
standfirst: A roundup of eight useful tips from Life Kit's August episodes. This month's edition includes a sweet goodbye ritual for children and advice on how to save more money at the grocery store.

title: What Biden’s tariffs on Chinese EVs and other products mean for U.S. consumers, jobs
standfirst: President Biden and former President Donald Trump have both embraced tariffs on foreign imports. We asked economist Sanjay Patnaik of the nonpartisan Brookings Institution what tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and other products mean for the U.S.

title: Should presidents have more of a say in interest rates?
standfirst: Former President Donald Trump recently suggested that if elected in this year's presidential election he would want more say on decisions made by the Federal Reserve. Presidents taking a more active role in monetary policy would mark an extraordinary shift in U.S. economic institutions, and mark the end of central bank independence.

title: What are Trump's economic plans?
standfirst: With less than two months before election day in the U.S., there's still a lot to learn about both major candidates' economic platforms. Today we look at some key proposals from Donald Trump for a second term, including tariffs and immigration. Tomorrow: Kamala Harris' plans.

title: What are Harris' economic plans?
standfirst: Yesterday we looked at Donald Trump's key economic proposals for a second term. On today's show, we do the same for Kamala Harris, examining the Democratic nominee's plans for taxes, housing and grocery store prices.

title: Inside the economic minds of the VP candidates
standfirst: Next week, JD Vance and Tim Walz will face off in the only confirmed vice presidential debate ahead of the election. As voters look ahead to what their economic policies might be, we look back to see what they have said and done, and how it turned out.

title: NPR listeners share their best money-saving grocery store tips
standfirst: Check your receipt. Grow your own veggies. Ask about senior discounts. NPR readers share their top tips on cutting costs at the grocery store.

title: Here are 4 ways the Federal Reserve's big rate cut could change the housing market
standfirst: Here's a look at what the Federal Reserve's rate cut will mean for those looking to buy — or sell — a home.

title: Are pharmacy benefit managers driving up drug prices? (Update)
standfirst: A group of obscure yet powerful players in the prescription drug industry are under the microscope. On Tuesday, at a Senate hearing in D.C., the head of pharmaceutical giant Novo Nordisk blamed the health insurance industry and pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, for allegedly making products like the weight loss drug Ozempic way more expensive in the U.S. than it is in other countries. A few days before that, the Federal Trade Commission sued three of the country's largest PBMs for allegedly using unfair tactics to artificially inflate the price of insulin.

title: U.K. is investigating Ticketmaster after Oasis tour prices surprised fans
standfirst: British regulators are looking into how Ticketmaster uses "dynamic pricing" to hike prices in line with demand. A similar controversy prompted a federal lawsuit against the company in the U.S.

title: Economic Lingo Bingo: Finally, a way to make a confusing election… fun!
standfirst: The team at Planet Money turned the economics terms being tossed out during the 2024 presidential campaign into a game of Economic Lingo Bingo!

title: Mail bag! Grad jobs, simplified branding and central bank independence
standfirst: Penny for your thoughts? Today we open our mail bag to hear from Indicator listeners. A college graduate tells us about their job search, a researcher discusses why products advertised as 'simple' may not be so straightforward, and another listener thinks the debate over Fed independence is a little more nuanced than we let on.

title: Rate Expectations: What it means that the Fed is about to lower interest rates.
standfirst: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates to get inflation under control. One side effect is that taking out a mortgage to buy a home has gotten very expensive. That's especially a problem for some homeowners who managed to get a lower mortgage rate years ago. They have a sort of... champagne problem. Or, "golden handcuffs" as it's called.

title: The latest jobs data provides a really confusing picture. Here are 4 things to know
standfirst: There was both good news — and bad news — in the latest jobs report, providing an unclear picture as the Federal Reserve weighs how much to cut interest rates.

title: America's small GDP bump, China's big stimulus dispersal, and a Monkey King
standfirst: It's time for ... Indicators of the Week! It is our show where we talk about fascinating numbers from the news. On today's episode, America's small GDP increase, a big assist from China's government to its lower income residents, and a high-grossing, centuries-old Monkey King.

title: Why the price of eggs is on the rise again
standfirst: The price of eggs has risen by about 28% in the past year, largely due to outbreaks of avian flu. Those prices could continue to climb during the holidays, as demand for baked goods increases.

title: The cost of living, lead pipe removal, and a more expensive Mega Millions
standfirst: It's ... Indicators of the Week! It's that time of week when we look at the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

title: Housing is expensive. Here's how Harris and Trump promise to bring costs down
standfirst: Housing costs are a top issue for many voters. Former President Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris have proposed different ideas for addressing the country's housing woes.

title: Mortgage rates were supposed to come down. Instead, they're rising. Here's why
standfirst: Mortgage rates are ticking up, even after the Federal Reserve has started cutting interest rates. Here's why, and where rates — and home sales — could go from here.

title: The U.S. once banned Chinese immigrants — and it paid an economic price
standfirst: In 1880, the Chinese were the biggest group of immigrants in the western U.S. But Sinophobic sentiments crystallized into racist policies and eventually the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. The rationale was that banning Chinese laborers would boost job opportunities for U.S.-born workers. Today, an economist explains how the Chinese exclusion laws affected the economies of western states and what it says about our current debate over immigration and jobs.

title: Where manufacturing jobs have shrunk, a library is giving a leg up to entrepreneurs
standfirst: The public library in Toledo, Ohio, is one of a number across the U.S. that have become entrepreneurial hubs. Business-specialist librarians are helping aspiring small-business owners and nonprofits for free.

title: The U.S. economy is growing solidly. Here's what's working — and what's not
standfirst: The U.S. economy grew at an annual rate of 2.8% in the third quarter, led by strong consumer spending. The news comes days before a presidential election in which the economy has been top of mind for many voters.

title: Why abortion referendums are also about the economy
standfirst: Abortion is on the ballot in 10 states. The vote results will have consequences beyond women's reproductive rights.

title: Why you’re seeing scary-high chocolate candy prices this Halloween
standfirst: Don't be surprised if you see fewer chocolate treats in your trick-or-treating loot. Customers are souring on costly chocolate, resulting from a few disappointing cocoa crop years.

title: Does unemployment whiplash mean recession?
standfirst: It's Jobs Friday! It's that time of the month where we check in on the American worker.

title: Port strikes end with deal on wages, averting economic disaster
standfirst: The two sides have agreed to a 62% wage increase over 6 years in a deal between the International Longshoremen's Association and the U.S. Maritime Alliance. The union had been seeking a 77% increase.

title: Tensions are rising in the Middle East, but the rise in oil prices is muted – so far
standfirst: Crude oil prices have risen as Iran and Israel trade attacks, but not as much as you might expect. One reason? OPEC+ could pump a lot more oil if it wanted to.

title: One possible housing crisis solution? A new kind of public housing for all income levels
standfirst: Maryland's Montgomery County is building mixed-income apartments in which people who can afford to pay market rate allow other renters to pay less. Cities and states nationwide are taking up the idea.

title: The U.S. saw stunningly strong growth in jobs last month. Here's what to know
standfirst: U.S. employers added more than a quarter million jobs in September, while the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. Here's what to know about the data.

title: The price America paid for its first big immigration crackdown
standfirst: The Chinese Exclusion Act was the first significant crackdown on immigration in American history. We explore the factors that led to the Act and examine what happened to the economy after it passed.

title: The story behind Cuba's economic dysfunction
standfirst: This week, a powerful hurricane hit Cuba, causing nationwide electricity outages — right after a string of power failures that have plagued the country in recent months. These power outages are a low point for a country that has struggled economically for years and is experiencing mass emigration.

title: Here's how minimum wage and paid sick leave measures fared in the election
standfirst: Some red states approved ballot measures to raise the minimum wage and require employers to provide paid sick time to their workers.

title: America's economy is the envy of the world. Will it stay that way?
standfirst: Donald Trump's victory in this year's election had a lot to do with how many Americans feel about the US economy (surprise: not good). But Simon Rabinovitch, US Economics Editor for The Economist, argues that, despite the turmoil of the past few years, America's economy remains the envy of the world. Today on the show, Simon explains why that is, but also why he believes a Trump presidency puts America's 'economic exceptionalism' at risk.

title: Fed up with high prices? Here's where things stand with inflation
standfirst: Inflation remains substantially lower than it did during its 2022 peak — but Americans are still frustrated with high prices.

title: Here's what Trump 2.0 means for the economy, from tariffs to mass deportations
standfirst: Trump has promised to cut taxes and government regulations, slap tariffs on imports and order large deportations of immigrants. Here's how that could impact the economy.

title: The Fed cuts interest rates -- but Trump's election could make things trickier
standfirst: The Federal Reserve cut interest rates by a quarter percentage point. How much further rates fall could depend on how President-elect Trump approaches his second term.

title: Trump's tariffs may be targeted at others -- but they could impact you too
standfirst: President-elect Donald Trump threatened to slap hefty tariffs on China, Canada and Mexico. Those tariffs would hurt America too — if they are carried out.

title: Are debt collectors calling you about a zombie 2nd mortgage?
standfirst: Old loans that homeowners thought were long dead have been rising from the grave as debt buyers move to collect. Some are allegedly breaking the law. If this is happening to you, tell us your story.

title: Why high prices toppled Democrats — and other governments around the world
standfirst: Voters really don't like inflation. In fact, whenever there's a sustained jump in the cost of living, the party in power often pays a price.

title: Canada's Trudeau says he had an 'excellent conversation' with Trump after tariffs threat
standfirst: The Canadian prime minister's meeting with Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago came after the president-elect's threat to impose tariffs on two of America's leading trade partners raised alarms.

title: Worst. Tariffs. Ever. (update)
standfirst: The Smoot Hawley Tariffs were a debacle that helped plunge America into the Great Depression. What can we learn from them?

title: Albertsons sues Kroger and ends failed grocery megamerger
standfirst: The lawsuit over a deal to combine the two largest U.S. supermarkets came just a day after it was blocked in both federal and Washington state courts.

title: Trump is all about tariffs as he leads a party that used to be all about free trade
standfirst: Once upon a time, Republicans spoke of free trade in glowing terms. With his constant threats of tariffs and a history of implementing them, President-elect Donald Trump has flipped that on its head.

title: Can empty-nesters boost housing affordability?
standfirst: The "silver tsunami" of aging Americans is often seen as a potential way to alleviate the country's housing affordability woes. However, the data suggests that an influx of empty-nester homes coming on the market won't have much of an impact on the problem—because of a geographical mismatch.

title: Businesses, shoppers brace for higher prices if tariffs on Mexico and Canada imports start Saturday
standfirst: President Trump renewed his threat to impose 25% tariffs on imports from Mexico and Canada as early as this weekend. The move could raise prices on everything from gasoline to guacamole.

title: Why Trump's tariff promises will be hard to keep
standfirst: President-elect Donald Trump has said his tariffs will raise revenues, boost U.S. jobs, and help stop the drug trade. But some of these goals are at odds with the others.

title: NPR shopped for 96 items at Walmart to track how prices are really changing
standfirst: NPR has tracked the prices of dozens of items at the same superstore in Georgia, including eggs, T-shirts, snacks and paper towels. Here's what got cheaper over the past year, and more expensive.

title: Local meteorologists could face layoffs amid new initiative with The Weather Channel
standfirst: The new initiative will be rolled out across 27 stations and feature "additional visual storytelling capabilities," Allen Media Group says.

title: The U.S. economy is still doing well as Americans continue to spend
standfirst: The U.S. economy grew at an annual rate of 2.3% in the final months of 2024, largely fueled by robust consumer spending. The economy ended the year 2.5% larger than it was a year earlier.

title: Running the numbers on deportation, interest rates and math
standfirst: Why haven't American 8th graders' math scores recovered? Does Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) actually have the resources to make all the deportations Trump's promised? And what's the path for interest rates in the Trump economy? All that on Indicators of the Week.

title: Trump's tariffs on Canada would be a big challenge for Americans, says ambassador
standfirst: Canada accounts for about 60% of U.S. crude oil imports. If Trump's tariffs end up applying to that oil, that would likely cause gas prices to rise in the U.S., Canada's ambassador warns.

title: China's exports in December up 10.7%, beating estimates as higher U.S. tariffs loom
standfirst: China has raced to fill orders ahead of President-elect Donald Trump's promised tariffs on Chinese goods. Exports have surged in the country since the pandemic.

title: CFPB sues Berkshire Hathaway-owned mortgage lender for alleged predatory practices
standfirst: The CFPB says that Vanderbilt Mortgage & Finance, owned by Berkshire Hathaway, ignored evidence that borrowers couldn't afford loans to buy manufactured homes.

title: How Trump's tariffs on steel and aluminum could hit you at the grocery store
standfirst: U.S. tariffs could cause the prices of steel and aluminum cans to rise, an increase that may ultimately be passed on to consumers.

title: What the cluck is happening with egg prices?
standfirst: We visit a local egg farm and talk to an industry analyst to get to the bottom of why the prices of eggs are soaring so quickly and when they might come back to earth.

title: IRS cuts over 6,000 jobs in the middle of tax season
standfirst: The IRS is cutting more than 6,000 jobs this week, as part of the Trump administration's downsizing of the overall federal workforce. The job cuts at the IRS come in the middle of the tax-filing season.

title: Up to 100 more workers are fired at CFPB as staff fear mass layoffs are looming
standfirst: About 70-100 employees were terminated at the CFPB, following dozens of recent workers who were fired earlier this week. Agency staff are bracing for even wider layoffs.

title: Here's a Super Bowl riddle: Why are egg prices surging — but not chicken wings?
standfirst: There is one economic riddle ahead of Super Bowl Sunday: The egg market has been hit hard by avian flu, but wings are abundant and relatively affordable this year. So what gives?

title: Trump threatens reciprocal tariffs against other countries
standfirst: President Trump is threatening to levy taxes on imports to match those other countries charge on U.S. exports.

title: A 24-hour 'economic blackout' is underway. Here's what to know
standfirst: The People's Union USA, a grassroots group, is calling on Americans to join a national boycott by not shopping for 24 hours on Friday.

title: Trump shifts date for Canada and Mexico tariffs — again
standfirst: Little about how Trump discusses tariffs is normal — not only because he threatens tariffs on a weekly, even daily, basis, but also because it's often unclear if or when those tariffs will happen.

title: The controversy over Tyson Foods' hiring of asylum seekers
standfirst: Last year, Tyson Foods shuttered a meat processing plant in Perry, Iowa. The company said it made the decision because the plant was old and inefficient. But the closure was devastating for the residents of Perry. The plant had employed some 1200 workers in a town with a population of only 8000.

title: Employers added fewer jobs in January -- but the labor market overall remains healthy
standfirst: U.S. employers added 143,000 jobs in January — a modest slowdown from the two previous months. The unemployment rate dipped to 4%.

title: At a housewares expo in Chicago, talk keeps turning to price hikes from tariffs
standfirst: The Inspired Home Show in Chicago draws housewares industry insiders from all over the country to network and show off their latest gadgets. This year, they're making plans to cope with tariffs.

title: PM x Radiolab: Can the economy grow forever?
standfirst: Earth can sustain life for another 100 million years, but can we? This episode, we partner with Radiolab to take stock of the essential raw materials that enable us to live as we do here on Earth — everything from sand to copper to oil — and tally up how much we have left. Are we living with reckless abandon? And if so, is there even a way to stop? A simultaneously terrifying and delightful conversation about bird poop, daredevil drivers, and some staggering back-of-the-envelope math.

title: When it comes to the economy, it's all about uncertainty
standfirst: Like a lot of economists, Mark Zandi, with Moody's Analytics, thinks President Trump's across-the-board tariffs are a bad idea. Saying, "Tariffs, broad-based tariffs, are a real problem for the economy."

title: A look at some of the creative ways companies try to dodge high tariffs
standfirst: Companies can try to avoid or minimize tariffs by requesting exemptions or legally reclassifying their products. Here's a look at some of the strategies that have worked in the past.

title: Trump says the economy is in 'transition.' What comes after?
standfirst: "A little disturbance," "a period of transition," "a detox period." These are all phrases that President Trump and his administration have used to describe the economy, as the stock market has plunged in response to one tariff announcement after another.

title: Trump threatens a 200% tariff on European alcohol
standfirst: European wines, champagne and other beverages could face heavy tariffs if Trump follows through with this threat.

title: The job market is still pretty solid — but there are warning signs ahead
standfirst: U.S. employers added 151,000 jobs in February, while the unemployment rate inched up to 4.1% from 4.0% in January.

title: Did tariffs contribute to the Great Depression? Here's what to know
standfirst: Several factors led to the Great Depression, one of the most severe economic crises in U.S. history. NPR interviewed economists who discussed the causes of the Great Depression.

title: As global tariff tensions rise, here's the latest on U.S. trade with top partners
standfirst: President Trump has upended global markets by imposing tariffs on imports from several of America's top trading partners. Here's what to know.

title: The Fed holds interest rates steady as Trump's trade agenda sparks uncertainty
standfirst: The Fed held rates steady, but left the door open to cut them later this year if inflation continues to ease. Trump's tariffs, however, could complicate efforts to bring prices under control.

title: Why CEOs are calm about tariffs in public — but 'very discouraged' in private
standfirst: Business leaders are trying to engage in a delicate diplomacy with the White House — even as their companies brace for the impact of market volatility and tariffs.

title: Can we just change how we measure GDP?
standfirst: There's one statistic that rules them all when it comes to keeping track of the economy: gross domestic product (GDP). It's the sum of all final transactions, so all the goods or services bought and sold, in an economy. GDP tells us how hot the economy is running, or how cool — like if we might be heading into a recession. And it's an important tool to compare countries, policies, and politicians. It's used by the U.S. government to allocate money and by businesses to make decisions about the future.

title: With Trump's crackdown on DEI, some women fear a path to good-paying jobs will close
standfirst: Some fear a setback for women and people of color after President Trump revoked a 1965 executive order that required federal contractors to identify and address barriers to employment.

title: Tesla, led by Elon Musk, warns of export retaliation due to new Trump tariffs
standfirst: Tesla has joined the ranks of U.S. companies concerned that Trump's aggressive tariff policies may negatively affect global sales.

title: Asian shares are sharply lower over concerns about the U.S. economy
standfirst: Asian shares were sharply lower on Monday as worries are building over a potentially toxic mix of worsening inflation and a U.S. economy slowing because households are cautious to spend.

title: Can ... we still trust the monthly jobs report?
standfirst: Between the Trump administration wanting to change how GDP is calculated and DOGE accessing sensitive government information, statistical agencies are under the microscope. Can we still trust official numbers like the monthly jobs report? A former Bureau of Labor Statistics commissioner shares her worries about the future integrity of government data.

title: The Fed holds interest rates. And, judge denies request to block DOGE's USIP takeover
standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady yesterday as concerns loom over President Trump's new tariffs. And, a judge denied a request to block DOGE's takeover of the U.S. Institute of Peace.

title: Southwest surprises, tariff guac shock, and fraud flourishes
standfirst: It's Indicators of the Week! Our weekly look at interesting numbers from the news.

title: Trump's latest tariff twist: A break for Mexico and Canada
standfirst: Trump put 25% tariffs on goods from Canada and Mexico on Tuesday. Markets tanked. And by Thursday, he had decided to broadly lift them.

title: Will tariffs drive more people to shop secondhand? It's a mixed bag, experts say
standfirst: This moment of economic uncertainty could drive more Americans to buy used. But experts say secondhand stores won't be immune from tariffs either.

title: How tariffs could impact the availability of baby products
standfirst: NPR's Mary Louise Kelly speaks with Steven Dunn founder and CEO of Munchkin a U.S.-based company selling lifestyle products for mothers, babies and children. Dunn has written an open letter to President Trump and Congress about how tariffs could harm his business and American families.

title: Trump closes loophole used by American shoppers to buy Chinese goods tariff-free
standfirst: The so-called de minimis exemption allowed Chinese and Hong Kong retailers to ship millions of packages worth $800 or less directly to U.S. consumers. That loophole will close May 2.

title: Smartphones and computers are now spared from Trump's reciprocal tariffs
standfirst: The exemption comes amid worries of how President Trump's steep new tariffs will affect American tech companies that rely on supply chains in China, like Apple.

title: Beijing slaps 125% tariffs on U.S. goods in latest U.S.-China trade escalation
standfirst: China signals the latest tariff hike will be its last round of tit-for-tat measures, prompting sharp falls in European shares, as Asian stocks end the day mixed.

title: Lipstick, sunscreen, & this podcast are recession indicators
standfirst: Global markets got a case of the jitters this week in the wake of President Trump's global tariff policy. Everyone from hedge fund managers to online content creators have been starting to question the stability of America's economic trajectory. We're now seeing increased fear that a recession is just around the corner.

title: Judge blocks mass layoffs at CFPB in the latest twist over the fate of the agency
standfirst: In declarations to federal court, CFPB employees describe a hasty process to eliminate most of the agency's staff. "[A]ll that matters is the numbers," one employee said they were told by leaders.

title: China put steep tariffs on U.S. exports. Farmers are worried
standfirst: The first Trump administration spent $28 billion bailing out farmers during a trade war with China. The White House has said it's starting to look at how to help this time around.

title: UAW President Shawn Fain explains why he supports Trump's tariffs
standfirst: Shawn Fein supports auto industry tariffs but calls broad tariffs "reckless."

title: Bracing for Trump's tariffs? Here are 3 money tips from a personal finance columnist
standfirst: President Trump's new taxes on imported goods are creating a "scary ride" for the U.S. market, says personal finance columnist Michelle Singletary. She recommends keeping these three things in mind.

title: 'Every day, every single customer': Tariffs hit close to home inside Asian grocers
standfirst: Asian grocery stores are a lifeline to the communities they serve. But store owners say the prospect of sweeping tariffs are threatening their ability to stock up on goods and keep prices affordable.

title: Between tariffs and survival, American business owners are doing alarming math
standfirst: Many U.S. shop owners feel like collateral damage in President Trump's trade war, on the hook to pay big new fees and long unable to manufacture in the U.S.

title: Trump is giving automakers a break on tariffs
standfirst: President Trump signed executive actions as the White House marks his 100 days in office. It's the latest shift in Trump's on-again, off-again approach to tariffs.

title: Jaguar and Land Rover maker pauses shipments to US as it develops post-tariff plans
standfirst: Jaguar Land Rover Automotive said it was pausing U.S. shipments due to Trump's tariffs as it works on mid- to long-term plans to adapt to the changing trade landscape.

title: Tariffs threaten to push auto insurance rates even higher
standfirst: Between the slate of tariffs currently in effect and proposed tariffs on car parts, the cost of car ownership is rising. And that's true even if you're not in the market for a vehicle.

title: Wall Street leaders warn of harsh economic consequences from Trump's tariffs
standfirst: The business sector has tried to avoid criticizing Trump in public and welcomed his vows of lower taxes and deregulation, but the market sell-off appears to have loosened more tongues on Wall Street.

title: The U.S. economy shrinks as Trump's tariffs spark recession fears
standfirst: Trump promised a new "golden age" for the U.S. But his first 100 days in office have left the economy looking tarnished, with data showing the economy contracted in the first three months of the year.

title: Sell USA? Why Trump's tariffs may be sparking a historic storm on Wall Street
standfirst: When Trump announced sweeping tariffs this month, he called it "Liberation Day." But there are fears that it may well have been the day foreign investors started to lose faith in the United States.

title: Are Trump's tariffs a bargaining chip for a new global economic order?
standfirst: It's not just tariffs. The White House is rethinking the central role of the dollar in the global economy.

title: Trump mulls semiconductor levies after lifting reciprocal tariffs on electronics
standfirst: Trump targets Chinese technology with 20% fentanyl tariff and eyes semiconductors in a "National Security Tariff Investigation" over coming months.

title: A major toy manufacturer is already nervous about Trump tariffs for holiday season
standfirst: Jay Foreman, CEO of Basic Fun!, says the Trump administration's shifting tariff policy has created chaos for businesses — and could still disrupt the holiday season.

title: World financial markets welcome court ruling against Trump's tariffs
standfirst: Financial markets welcomed a U.S. court ruling that blocks President Trump from imposing sweeping tariffs on imports under an emergency-powers law.

title: USDA chief says agency is trying to fill key jobs after paying 15,000 to leave
standfirst: Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins says the department will consider bringing back some employees who took the government's deferred resignation offer.

title: Sellers of dog leashes and mom gear hope court rulings lead to tariff relief
standfirst: Court rulings against President Trump's tariffs could spell relief for many American importers — if the decisions hold. For now, the uncertainty remains.

title: Advice for navigating a volatile economy
standfirst: The U.S. economy is in flux. And for millions of Americans, a new line item in their budget includes repaying federal student loans.

title: Why aren't Americans filling the manufacturing jobs we already have?
standfirst: Leaders from both major political parties have been working to bring back manufacturing. But American manufacturers say they are struggling to fill the manufacturing jobs we already have.

title: Why an economist says temporary U.S.-China tariff deal doesn't ease uncertainty
standfirst: Businesses are rushing to import Chinese goods after the U.S. struck a temporary deal. This "stop-go" nature of trade could still mean higher prices and doesn't ease uncertainty, an economist warns.

title: How economists (and TikTok) know if a recession is coming
standfirst: Lately we've noticed that something we think about all the time here at Planet Money is having a viral moment: recession indicators!

title: Stocks soar after U.S. and China agree to temporarily slash tariffs
standfirst: Stocks rallied after the U.S. and China said they would slash tariffs on each other's imports for 90 days.

title: Why do shrimpers like tariffs?
standfirst: Many businesses are scared of what President Trump's tariffs will mean for their industry. However, the shrimping industry is one that doesn't seem to be worried. In fact, shrimpers say they welcome them. On today's episode, why shrimpers are embracing the tariffs and whether economists agree that this tariff is good for Americans.

title: How a visit from actor Jon Voight led Trump to post about movie tariffs
standfirst: Since he announced his intention to impose a 100% tariff on movies made outside of the United States, President Trump has hedged, saying he's open to meeting with industry leaders.

title: Home Depot doesn't plan to raise prices due to tariffs. But some items may disappear
standfirst: The home improvement chain broke from many other retailers, who say they cannot afford to absorb new tariffs. President Trump recently attacked Walmart for warning of price hikes.

title: In the wake of tariffs, cargo at the Port of LA is down 35%
standfirst: The immediate impact of the cargo decline affects virtually every business around the ports, but port officials say this downturn will soon be felt much more broadly.

title: The Fed holds interest rates steady as Trump's tariffs spark uncertainty
standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday as President Trump's tariffs threaten to raise prices and drag down economic growth.

title: Despite the pause on high tariffs, Chinese factories still face high uncertainty
standfirst: A 90-day pause on triple-digit U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods has left exporters and importers in a high state of uncertainty. Factory owners in China tell NPR that orders are down overall.

title: U.S. egg prices fall for the first time in months but remain near record highs
standfirst: The average price for a dozen Grade A eggs declined to $5.12 last month after reaching a record $6.23 in March. It was the first month-to-month drop in egg prices since October 2024.

title: Inflation cools in April — but tariffs could upend the picture in coming months
standfirst: Consumer prices in April were up 2.3% from a year ago, the smallest annual increase in more than four years. Grocery prices fell 0.4%, thanks to a large drop in the price of eggs.

title: First, relief. Then, a scramble to get stuff in after U.S. cuts China tariffs for now
standfirst: Although business owners welcomed a temporary deal with China to slash tariffs, there's still considerable uncertainty about what happens next.

title: Can retailers eat tariffs without price hikes? Walmart, Target, Lowe's face pressure
standfirst: Major chains are fighting two battles at once: a financial battle to keep costs low in the face of new tariffs, and a political one to avoid the president's wrath.

title: Basic Fun! CEO warns tariffs could double toy prices, threaten Christmas sales
standfirst: Toymakers say they will have to raise prices to offset Trump's tariffs. NPR's Michel Martin speaks with Jay Foreman, CEO of Basic Fun!, whose toys include Care Bears, Tonka Trucks and Lincoln Logs.

title: Hiring slowed in May, as employers added 139,000 jobs
standfirst: U.S. employers added 139,000 jobs in May — a modest slowdown from the previous month. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.2%, as the workforce shrank.

title: With steel tariffs doubling today, a North Carolina manufacturer wonders how to compete
standfirst: President Trump is doubling tariffs on steel and aluminum to 50%. It's designed to protect domestic steel and aluminum workers, but critics say it will raise prices for those that use the metals.

title: Fed holds interest rates steady, signals rate cuts of 0.5% later this year
standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday. Members of the central bank's rate-setting committee also telegraphed their plans for possible rate cuts later this year.

title: Are Trump's tariffs legal?
standfirst: When President Trump announced his sweeping new tariffs this year, many trade law experts were startled. Typically, presidents don't have the authority to impose broad tariffs with a snap of their fingers.

title: Steel tariffs double. And, Congress asked to eliminate public broadcasting funds
standfirst: Tariffs on imported steel and aluminum are doubling today. Here's how it could impact your wallets. And, Trump has asked Congress to wipe out funding for public broadcasting.

title: Canada ditches digital tax after tariff threat from Trump
standfirst: Canada scrapped a digital services tax that would have hit U.S. tech companies such as Google and Amazon after President Trump halted trade talks and threatened higher tariffs on Canadian imports.

title: Why some economists are worried about U.S. inflation data
standfirst: The federal government is scaling back data collection used to calculate the inflation rate because of staff shortages. Economists warn that could make for less accurate cost-of-living measures.

title: Sen. Tim Kaine says Trump's tariffs could reduce federal debt, but at what cost?
standfirst: NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., who is also on the Senate Budget Committee, about how President Trump's tariffs will affect the federal budget and the economy.

title: Here comes the bridal gown tariff
standfirst: How much extra would you pay to see your dream come true? It's always a big question for wedding-planning couples. Now, there's a new twist courtesy of U.S. trade policy.

title: Less bang for your buck: Even the July 4 fireworks may be hit by tariffs this year
standfirst: Fans of fireworks may face higher prices this Fourth of July. That's because most fireworks are made in China and importers now have to pay tariffs of at least 30%.

title: The hidden costs of healthcare churn
standfirst: Healthcare churn—when people switch insurance plans—is particularly bad in the US.

title: Trump's tariffs could cut deficit by $2.8 trillion over next decade -- with caveats
standfirst: The Congressional Budget Office projected President Trump's tariffs could raise trillions of dollars over the next decade — but they could also lead to higher inflation and slower economic growth.

title: Inflation is holding steady as Trump's tariffs have yet to fully hit
